title: Trump DOJ attempts to end citizenship for indigenous families
description_short: Trump DOJ attempts to end citizenship for indigenous families
description_medium: In January 2025, the Trump administration argued in court that the 14th Amendment’s citizenship clause may not cover Indigenous people who owe allegiance to tribal nations. The Justice Department made the argument while defending Trump’s birthright-citizenship executive order. A federal judge blocked the order, and the timeline notes that U.S. law has long recognized tribal citizens as U.S. citizens as well.
description_long: The Justice Department made the argument in a court filing opposing a request to block Trump’s executive order ending birthright citizenship. The filing relied on the 14th Amendment’s phrase “subject to the jurisdiction” of the United States and cited Elk v. Wilkins, a 19th-century Supreme Court case involving a member of a Native nation. The timeline says the administration argued that Indigenous people who owe immediate allegiance to their tribes may fall outside the citizenship clause. The argument was part of litigation over the executive order; it was not itself a change in citizenship law or a court ruling that Native Americans are not U.S. citizens. A federal judge in Washington blocked the order, and the source notes that the U.S. government has recognized tribal citizens as citizens for more than 150 years. The episode raised concern because the administration’s reading could reach beyond the order’s stated target and affect Indigenous families. The record describes a legal position advanced by the government and the judge’s response, while distinguishing both from settled constitutional law or an implemented loss of citizenship.

title: Trump: ICE ships Palestinians to Israel on Trump buddy's jet
description_short: Trump: ICE ships Palestinians to Israel on Trump buddy's jet
description_medium: On January 21, 2026, ICE flew eight Palestinian men from Arizona to Israel on a private jet owned by real-estate developer Gil Dezer, a longtime Trump associate and donor. The timeline reported that the men arrived shackled in Tel Aviv and were taken to the Israeli-occupied West Bank. It said the operation was repeated in early February and that the administration did not explain the cost of using Dezer’s aircraft.
description_long: Immigration and Customs Enforcement carried out a flight on January 21, 2026, transporting eight Palestinian men from Arizona to Israel aboard a luxury jet owned by Gil Dezer. The timeline identifies Dezer as a longtime Trump friend whose family developed Trump-branded properties and who contributed to Trump’s campaigns. It reports that the men arrived in Tel Aviv with their hands and ankles shackled and were taken to the Israeli-occupied West Bank without food, water, or shelter. The source says a similar operation was repeated in early February and that this was at least the sixth deportation flight using Dezer’s aircraft. It did not identify every passenger; it noted that at least one had lived in the United States since adolescence and had a newborn child. The Guardian was cited for reporting that the administration would not answer how much ICE paid to use the plane; aviation sources estimated a flight could cost $400,000 to $500,000. These details are reported claims, not a complete public manifest or accounting. The entry documents an unusual removal route, the private aircraft connection, and questions about the treatment of the passengers and public cost.

title: Trump: Russia's Internet Research Agency shifts focus to the U.S. election
description_short: Trump: Russia's Internet Research Agency shifts focus to the U.S. election
description_medium: In April 2014, Russia’s Internet Research Agency formed a “translator project” focused on U.S. election interference, according to reporting cited by the timeline. The agency was organized like a newsroom, with graphics, data-analysis, search-optimization, IT, and finance departments. Its leadership changed that month, and reporting connected the agency’s funding to Concord, a company associated with Yevgeny Prigozhin.
description_long: The Internet Research Agency began organizing a “translator project” in April 2014 to work on efforts directed at the U.S. election, according to the reporting cited by the timeline. The source describes an operation built with departments for graphics, data analysis, search optimization, information technology, and finance, resembling a newsroom designed to produce and distribute false material. It says Mikhail Bystrov took over leadership that month. The agency had been founded in 2013 and was funded by Concord Management and Consulting. Russian media reports and investigations linked Concord to Yevgeny Prigozhin, a business figure close to the Kremlin, though the timeline notes that parts of that funding relationship were attributed to reporting rather than official confirmation at the time. The entry traces an early organizational step in Russian influence activity before the 2016 election. It provides context for later investigations into online interference but does not show that the project alone determined an election outcome or that Trump’s campaign directed the agency. Its central event is the formation of a specialized team and infrastructure for targeting U.S. audiences.

title: Trump Admin blocks $455 billion in COVID aid from Biden
description_short: Trump Admin blocks $455 billion in COVID aid from Biden
description_medium: On November 25, 2020, Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin said the department would return unused CARES Act funds that had supported Federal Reserve emergency lending programs. The amount at issue was $455 billion in Treasury backing, not direct relief checks. Mnuchin also moved to close five lending facilities, prompting disagreement with the Federal Reserve and criticism from advisers to the incoming Biden administration.
description_long: The dispute concerned unused Treasury funds authorized by the CARES Act to support Federal Reserve emergency lending facilities during the COVID-19 pandemic. Treasury Secretary Steven Mnuchin said he would return $455 billion in remaining funds and close five programs near the end of 2020. The amount represented Treasury capital backing that could support Federal Reserve lending; it was not $455 billion in direct payments to households. The Federal Reserve publicly objected to ending the programs, saying it preferred that the full set of facilities remain available while the economy was still vulnerable. Jerome Powell said the central bank was not ready to close them. Bharat Ramamurti, a member of the congressional committee overseeing CARES Act funds, called Mnuchin’s move illegal and argued it could limit the incoming Biden administration’s options for responding to the pandemic. The programs had seen relatively little use, but supporters viewed them as a backstop for credit markets and businesses. The entry records the funding dispute, the Treasury’s decision, and the disagreement between Mnuchin and the Federal Reserve. It does not assert that the funds were direct household aid or that their return alone prevented later relief legislation.

title: Trump: Bondi tells Trump he appears on Epstein list multiple times
description_short: Trump: Bondi tells Trump he appears on Epstein list multiple times
description_medium: According to the timeline, Attorney General Pam Bondi told Trump in May 2025 that his name appeared multiple times in Epstein-related documents and briefed him on other prominent names. A later Wall Street Journal report described the material as unverified hearsay. In July, the Justice Department said its review found no “client list” and no basis for further investigation; an appearance in records does not itself imply wrongdoing.
description_long: The timeline says Attorney General Pam Bondi met with Trump in May 2025 and told him that his name appeared multiple times in documents related to Jeffrey Epstein. It also says Bondi discussed other high-profile names in the files. A Wall Street Journal report published in July described what Trump had been told as unverified hearsay about multiple people, including Trump. On July 6, the Justice Department and FBI released a statement saying their review found no Epstein “client list” and no evidence warranting further investigation or prosecution. That later statement sits in tension with the public expectation that a definitive list of clients existed. The entry records a reported briefing and subsequent government statement; it does not establish that Trump committed a crime, that his name appeared in a particular evidentiary context, or that the documents contained verified allegations against every named person. The distinction matters because a person’s name appearing in investigative records is not itself evidence of criminal conduct. The episode became a public controversy over what the government’s review had found and what officials had previously suggested about the files.

title: Trump: Jacob Wohl and Jack Burkman frame Dr. Fauci for sexual assault
description_short: Trump: Jacob Wohl and Jack Burkman frame Dr. Fauci for sexual assault
description_medium: In April 2020, Jacob Wohl and lobbyist Jack Burkman promoted a sexual-assault allegation against Dr. Anthony Fauci through a woman using the name Diana Rodriguez. Later reporting identified her as Diana Andrade and reported that she said she had been paid to participate. The lawyers named in the initial release could not be verified. The allegation against Fauci was not substantiated.
description_long: Jacob Wohl and Jack Burkman issued a press release in April 2020 featuring a woman who accused Dr. Anthony Fauci of sexual assault in 2014. She was identified as Diana Rodriguez, but later reporting found that the person using that name did not exist and that the lawyers listed in the release could not be verified. The woman was identified as Diana Andrade, who told Reason that she had known Wohl and accepted money to take part in the effort. She also said Wohl and Burkman had asked her to participate in a similar stunt earlier and were seeking another accuser. The source reports that the allegation against Fauci was fabricated and that the publicized accuser later withdrew the claim. Fauci was a prominent public-health official during the early COVID-19 response, so the false accusation risked diverting attention from that work and damaging his reputation. The entry documents the campaign by Wohl and Burkman, the false identity used, and Andrade’s account of her participation. It does not repeat the initial allegation as fact; no evidence was presented in the supplied reporting to substantiate a sexual assault by Fauci.

Phelan led private-equity firm MSD Capital and was known as an art collector; the supplied account says he had not served in the military or led a service branch. It also reports that Phelan hosted a fundraising dinner for Trump at his Aspen home, with tickets priced from $25,000 to $500,000 per couple.
